Lisbon. The capital and largest city of Portugal, strategically positioned on the Tagus River estuary where it meets the Atlantic Ocean.

Located on the Tagus estuary, which provided a natural harbor and protected anchorage for oceangoing vessels, Lisbon was positioned perfectly at the convergence of river and sea. It rose to prominence in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries as the center of Portuguese maritime expansion and colonial ambition, becoming Europe's gateway to the world.

Home to the Portuguese monarchy and government, the palaces and archives reflect centuries of imperial power and cultural achievement. Lisbon served as the point of departure for Vasco da Gama's voyage to India in fourteen ninety-seven, which established the sea route to Asia and transformed global trade forever.

The city was devastated by a catastrophic earthquake in seventeen fifty-five that destroyed much of the medieval city. It was rebuilt in a rational, grid-based plan by Marquês de Pombal. Through control of Atlantic and Indian Ocean trade, Lisbon became one of the most important hubs of the Age of Exploration and a symbol of European ambition.

Fado music, a melancholic national tradition, originated in Lisbon's working-class neighborhoods and remains central to Portuguese identity and cultural expression worldwide.
